newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh PM appeals for consensus on reforms.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh PM appeals for consensus on reforms.

text.p: Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, seeking to confront a growing opposition challenge, on Wednesday sought public cooperation to usher in public sector reforms.
"Let us remain united irrespective of political differences in the nation-building activities," she told a workshop in Dhaka.
Hasina repeated her Awami League government's commitment to reform the public administration, often branded corrupt and inefficient. She said a committee would be formed to make recommendations.
The finance ministry arranged the workshop to discuss a recent World Bank report that recommended sweeping reforms if Bangladesh is to attain a goal of seven percent growth in the next two years.
Current annual gross domestic product growth is about five percent.

The government has yet to spell out specific reforms, but officials say she would stress strengthening local government, curbing bureaucracy and rewriting business laws to help the private sector flourish in line with government policy.
Hasina, who took office following general elections in June, said public organisations were not "up to the mark" and public bodies were incurring losses due to mismanagement and inefficiency.
"It (the public sector) cannot be a great help in achieving economic growth when the public organisations are poorly managed," she said.
Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria called for consensus among major political parties to make reforms "take root".
"Reforms were either left half done or could not be started in the past due to a lack of consensus," he said.
World Bank South Asia director Dr Mieko Nishimizu suggested strong leadership for public sector reforms to work.
"Bangladesh surely can't afford a wrong kind of government especially when we (World Bank) project a future of shrinking concessional aid resources," Nishimizu said.
Overseas donors, including the World Bank, give Bangladesh around $2.0 billion a year.
